title: Writing Numbers in Other Bases
short: Convert to base b by dividing by b again and again, then read the remainders from last to first.
trouble: Students write the remainders in the order they found them, which puts the digits backward.

blocks.html: We write numbers in base 10: $2024$ means $2 \cdot 10^{3} + 0 \cdot 10^{2} + 2 \cdot 10 + 4$. Nothing is special about ten except our fingers. Computers use base 2, programmers use base 16, and the division algorithm is exactly the tool for moving between bases.

Base $b$. Fix an integer $b \ge 2$. Every positive integer $n$ can be written in exactly one way as $$n = d_k b^{k} + d_{k-1} b^{k-1} + \cdots + d_1 b + d_0,$$ with digits $0 \le d_i \le b - 1$ and $d_k \neq 0$. We write $n = (d_k d_{k-1} \dots d_0)_b$, or $d_k \dots d_0$ with a subscript $b$. Base 16 needs six extra digits: A = 10, B = 11, …, F = 15.

Divide $n$ by $b$: every term except $d_0$ is a multiple of $b$, so $$n = b\,(d_k b^{k-1} + \cdots + d_1) + d_0, \qquad 0 \le d_0 < b.$$ By the uniqueness in the division algorithm, $d_0$ is the remainder of $n$ divided by $b$, and the quotient is the number whose digits are $d_k \dots d_1$. Repeat on the quotient and the remainders peel off the digits one at a time, last digit first. That same uniqueness is why the digits are unique.

blocks.title: Decimal to binary
steps: $2 = 2 \cdot 1 + 0$, and $1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1$. Stop when the quotient is $0$.
The remainders were $0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1$. Read them from the last to the first: $101100$.

blocks.title: Hexadecimal to decimal
steps: The digits are $2$, $\mathrm{F} = 15$ and $3$, standing for $16^{2}$, $16^{1}$ and $16^{0}$.

head: Power of 2
blocks.cap: Place values in base 2. Each hex digit stands for 4 binary digits, since $16 = 2^{4}$.

blocks.html: Writing the remainders in the order you found them. For $44$ that gives $001101_2 = 13$, not $44$: the first remainder is the ones digit, which goes on the right. Always check by expanding the answer back into base 10.

Base 16 is popular because it is a shorthand for base 2: split the binary digits into groups of four from the right and replace each group by one hex digit. For example $101100_2 = 0010\ 1100_2 = \mathrm{2C}_{16}$, since $0010_2 = 2$ and $1100_2 = 12 = \mathrm{C}$. Check: $2 \cdot 16 + 12 = 44$.
Binary will come back in fast powers, where the binary digits of an exponent tell you which squares to multiply.
To write $n$ in base $b$, divide by $b$ again and again; the remainders are the digits, from the ones digit up. To go back, multiply each digit by its power of $b$ and add.
